query: For high-entropy alloys intended for aerospace fasteners, what single intervention could improve the combination of mechanical durability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence that supports it, and an experiment with clear results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a moderate amount of molybdenum (around 5–10 at.%) during alloy fabrication will improve the mechanical durability, enhance room‐temperature creep resistance, and boost corrosion resistance of high-entropy alloys for aerospace fasteners.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline high-entropy alloy (HEA) produced without Mo addition that exhibits conventional grain boundary morphology, standard precipitation (if any), and moderate corrosion behavior.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled 5–10 at.% Mo addition (via powder-based directed energy deposition) into the HEA composition during processing, with post-processing heat treatment designed to allow controlled cooling.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature mechanical testing and simulated aerospace environments (e.g., mild saline or chloride-containing conditions that mimic airborne corrosive exposures).
generation.structural_mediator: The Mo addition is expected to modify the microstructure by promoting the formation of serrated (undulated) grain boundaries and refined secondary phases (such as stable σ or γ′ particles), while also enriching grain boundary regions in Mo that support the formation of a dense, stable oxide film.
generation.mechanism: Molybdenum acts by both inducing subtle changes in grain boundary morphology (leading to serration that disperses local strain concentrations, thereby inhibiting creep and intergranular cracking) and improving solid-solution as well as precipitation strengthening. In addition, Mo’s tendency to segregate at boundaries promotes the development of a protective passivating layer, reducing corrosion rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated baseline alloy, the Mo-alloyed variant should exhibit increased yield strength and improved mechanical durability, demonstrate a lower steady-state creep strain rate or longer time to creep rupture at room temperature, and show a marked decrease in corrosion current density (indicating better passivation) under corrosive test conditions.
generation.baseline: The original HEA without Mo, which has lower yield strength, normal (or even elevated) localized creep deformation at room temperature, and moderate corrosion resistance when exposed to aggressive environments.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected only if the Mo content is maintained at moderate levels (around 5–10 at.%) and the processing (including the cooling rate in post heat treatment) allows for the controlled formation of beneficial microstructural features. Excessive Mo or non-optimized thermal treatments might lead to unwanted brittle intermetallics that could counteract these benefits.
generation.uncertainty: The combined microstructural effects of Mo—namely, the induction of serrated grain boundaries (as shown in PMC9848264) and enhancements in corrosion and yield strength (as demonstrated in PMC11509674)—suggest this dual benefit. However, the exact quantitative improvement in room-temperature creep resistance and its transferability to fastener-scale components in aerospace applications remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy fastener prototypes using the same additive manufacturing method (e.g., DED): one set with the baseline composition and one with an additional 5–10 at.% Mo. Subject both sets to identical post-heat treatment routines (with a controlled, slower cooling rate) to promote the beneficial microstructural evolution. Then perform room-temperature tensile tests, constant-load creep tests under service-relevant stress levels, and potentiodynamic polarization tests in a simulated corrosive (e.g., saline) environment.
measurements: Yield strength and fracture strain from tensile tests
Steady-state creep strain rate or time-to-rupture under constant load at room temperature
Corrosion current density, passivation and pitting potentials from electrochemical tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-alloyed samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements relative to the baseline (for example, less than a 10% increase in yield strength, minimal change in creep performance, or less than a 20% reduction in corrosion current density) across repeated tests, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHighly entropy alloys (HEAs) are novel materials that have great potential for application in aerospace and marine engineering due to their superior mechanical properties and benefits over conventional materials. NiCrCoFe, also referred to as Ni-based HEA, has exceptional low-temperature strength and microstructural stability. However, HEAs have limited corrosion resistance in some environments, such as a 3.5 wt% sodium chloride (NaCl) solution. Adding corrosion-resistant elements such as molybdenum (Mo) to HEAs is expected to increase their corrosion resistance in a variety of corrosive environments. Metal additive manufacturing reduces production times compared to casting and eliminates shrinkage issues, making it ideal for producing homogeneous HEA. This study used directed energy deposition (DED) to create Cr25-xCo25Ni25Fe25Mox (x = 0, 5, 10%) HEAs. Tensile strength and potentiodynamic polarization tests were used to assess the materials’ mechanical properties and corrosion resistance. ABSTRACTIn this study, tensile and creep deformation of a high-entropy alloy processed by selective laser melting (SLM) has been investigated; hot ductility drop was identified at first, and the loss of ductility at elevated temperature was associated with intergranular fracture. By modifying the grain boundary morphology from straight to serration, the hot ductility drop issue has been resolved successfully. The serrated grain boundary could be achieved by reducing the cooling rate of solution heat treatment, which allowed the coarsening of L12 structured γ′ precipitates to interfere with mobile grain boundaries, resulting in undulation of the grain boundary morphology. Tensile and creep tests at 650°C were conducted, and serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively. Detailed microstructure analysis has indicated that serrated grain boundary could distribute strains more evenly than that of straight morphology.
